name: Power Grid

claims.claim_text: Grid frequency is the signal that says whether generation matches load. Every generator tracks it in a feedback loop, so the balance between supply and demand is communicated across the entire system by a single physical quantity that every participant can measure locally.
claims.quote_verbatim: the frequency is what determines if you have enough generation or not
claims.speaker: Paul Zawada
claims.episode_title: The Smart Grid with Paul Zawada

claims.claim_text: Control is layered and distributed. Balancing authorities — sometimes non-profit entities, sometimes utilities — ensure generation matches load at a high level, while minute-by-minute regulation happens inside each generator's own control system, whether that is a steam turbine, a wind turbine or a solar inverter.
claims.quote_verbatim: lot of times those are called balancing authorities
claims.speaker: Paul Zawada
claims.episode_title: The Smart Grid with Paul Zawada

claims.claim_text: Energy entering the grid joins a pool. No particular joule can be traced from a specific plant to a specific load, which is why claims about consuming power from one source are statements about accounting rather than about physics.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't trace a specific jewel of energy provided by one plant
claims.speaker: Paul Zawada
claims.episode_title: The Smart Grid with Paul Zawada

claims.claim_text: Operational technology is a distinct discipline from both power engineering and information technology: the computing and communications that attach to physical plant. The same skills apply across power, transportation and pipelines, and the work sits precisely where embedded systems meet equipment measured in megawatts.
claims.quote_verbatim: operational technology is kind of that computing and communication stuff that gets wired to the physical devices
claims.speaker: Paul Zawada
claims.episode_title: The Smart Grid with Paul Zawada

claims.claim_text: The interconnected grid is plausibly the largest and most complex machine ever built, and it is also an unglamorous industry that struggles to attract engineers — a combination that matters because the expertise is not easily replaced.
claims.quote_verbatim: isn't the grid, the largest single construction on earth
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Smart Grid with Paul Zawada

claims.claim_text: There is no central authority operating the grid. National energy policy works by incentivising technologies that make it more efficient, more reliable and less in need of upgrades, which means change arrives through economics rather than through instruction.
claims.quote_verbatim: to incentivize new technologies that can be deployed to make the grid
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: A utility's real interest in an interconnection application, beyond installation safety, is retaining the ability to shut the generation off. A feeder carrying more supply than local load is a genuine problem, and curtailment is the mechanism of last resort.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the event that a feeder has too much supply and not enough load
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: When distributed generation exceeds what a feeder can absorb, the available responses begin with curtailment — simply turning the generation down — which is the outcome least attractive to the owner and cheapest for everyone else.
claims.quote_verbatim: the utility can curtail it
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: A microgrid is not simply sharing power with neighbours. It is a defined sub-portion of the larger grid that can be understood and operated as a unit — which is what makes it a planning tool rather than a description of what already happens between adjacent houses.
claims.quote_verbatim: the microgrid, that term
claims.speaker: Ari Gerstman
claims.episode_title: Renewable Energy Policy with Ari Gerstman

claims.claim_text: Generators earn disproportionately at peak: bringing an extra turbine online on a hot afternoon commands the highest rates of the year, and the steady baseload business is comparatively unremarkable. Solar arriving precisely at that afternoon peak therefore attacks the most profitable hours rather than the average ones, which is why it disrupts grid economics faster than its share of energy suggests.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of their money is made actually at peak times
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: Distributed generation behaves like bulk capacitance on the system: it smooths the ripples as loads switch on and off and adds capacity where it is consumed. The analogy also explains what is lost when the economics stop supporting it.
claims.quote_verbatim: that would be, like, the, you know, the bulk capacitance for the system
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: Operators object to renewable generation on the grounds of intermittency rather than on principle. What a grid is built to do is match a varying load with controllable supply, and a supply that varies independently of load makes that job harder.
claims.quote_verbatim: grid operators don't like renewables
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: Nuclear generation is designed for steady state: start it and run it until refuelling, avoiding fast changes in anything. That makes it the opposite of the newer intermittent sources in the specific respect that matters to an operator — it is consistent, and it does not follow load.
claims.quote_verbatim: the whole goal of nuclear power is steady state
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Wait, why is Jeff glowing?

claims.claim_text: A whole-state blackout followed a severe storm taking down major interconnectors, automated protection tripping correctly, and insufficient internal capacity to carry the load alone. Robustness is a property of how the system is architected — including how much local generation can stand alone — rather than of the generation mix in isolation.
claims.quote_verbatim: that took down a couple of major power lines
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Decoupled Episode

claims.claim_text: A major grid failure traced back to frozen natural gas lines, because gas provides much of the fast-responding instantaneous generation. The lesson generalises: a grid's resilience depends on the fuel supply chains beneath it, which are rarely modelled alongside the electrical system.
claims.quote_verbatim: of the root causes of that was that the natural gas lines froze
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pneumatic Tubes, Straight To The Home

claims.claim_text: Industrial loads reach a scale where a single site is a grid-level actor: an aluminium smelter paying seven million dollars a month for electricity had monitoring on its incoming supply because a large motor going to ground could force the shutdown of a substantial fraction of that state's grid.
claims.quote_verbatim: their electricity bill per month was, uh, $7 million a month
claims.speaker: John Davis
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Davis

claims.claim_text: A single domestic appliance switching on is noise once a thousand houses are in parallel — people switch off as others switch on and the aggregate is smooth. The loads that actually move the system are industrial, such as a factory bringing its lighting up at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're talking about, you know, a thousand houses hooked in parallel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Senseless Saccadic Shemozzle

claims.claim_text: Remotely controllable appliances create a new class of coordinated demand step. If a large population of connected air conditioners could be commanded on simultaneously, the resulting demand appears instantly rather than following the diurnal curve the system is designed around.
claims.quote_verbatim: if somebody could hack all those at once and turn them all on
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: Geomagnetic disturbance remains a live disaster scenario for transmission infrastructure, with historical precedent for a single event affecting the grids of multiple countries — a risk that scales with the length of the conductors rather than with the sophistication of the equipment attached.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're solar flare vulnerable
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Reliability varies enormously by region and is worth quantifying before generalising: one major metropolitan grid has never gone down in its entirety in fifty years, with outages confined to pockets of tens of thousands of customers for under a day.
claims.quote_verbatim: anyone remember the entire, uh, Sydney Basin ever going down? And the answer is no
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Decoupled Episode

claims.claim_text: What modern infrastructure depends on is not electricity but its consistency: power available instantly, constantly and cheaply, such that flicking a switch is not a decision. Consistency rather than capacity is the property that separates a functioning grid from a nominal one.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of our modern society relies on the fact that we get instant, constant, cheap power
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gouging Green Gardyloo

claims.claim_text: Under net metering, generation consumed on site never reaches the meter while the excess is exported at a much lower rate than importing costs. The rational response is to move consumption into the generating hours — running the washing machine at midday — because using your own energy is worth more than selling it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the way our solar panel works is it uses net metering
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Factories and HVDC Lines - Pollent Power Pushing

claims.claim_text: Older installations used two separate meters, one counting import and one counting export, where a modern smart meter reports both through a portal as a daily figure. That daily record is what makes it possible to notice a small persistent anomaly at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: would have an import meter and an export meter
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Watt Is The Deal

claims.claim_text: A battery inverter typically has a programmable trickle setting that draws a small continuous amount from the grid to keep the connection alive. Anyone investigating an unexplained standing import should check that setting first, and can test the hypothesis directly by changing it and watching whether the daily figure moves proportionally.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have this on-grid trickle feature where you can actually program
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Watt Is The Deal

claims.claim_text: A small persistent discrepancy in energy accounting may simply be the meter: at roughly one percent tolerance, an apparent standing import of a fraction of a kilowatt-hour a day can fall inside the instrument's specification, which is unsatisfying and is a real answer.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe it could be with inside the 1% tolerance of the meter
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Watt Is The Deal

claims.claim_text: Grids are not one system even within a country — one large state operates a grid deliberately separate from its neighbours — and internationally the differences extend to phase arrangements and frequency. Even physically interconnected regions can run incompatible metering standards.
claims.quote_verbatim: in Texas, the grid is completely separate from the rest of the United States
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Watt Is The Deal

claims.claim_text: A well-to-wheels accounting that followed the diesel for the mining equipment, the transport, the generation, a 7.5 percent delivery loss to the garage and the charging loss found 27 percent less carbon dioxide per mile than a gallon of petrol — even assuming every kilowatt-hour came from coal, and at a measured 3.5 miles per kilowatt-hour taken from the grid.
claims.quote_verbatim: 27% less CO2 produced if 100% of the energy that I drive with came from coal
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: Electrifying transport is a grid problem more than a vehicle problem: moving that power through the network requires building new infrastructure and retiring old, and industry estimates of how long that takes have compressed from decades to a small number of years — which is itself a source of planning risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: how we build in new pieces of infrastructure and potentially even remove old parts of infrastructure
claims.speaker: Eric Klein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: Against a genuinely reliable grid, domestic battery storage is difficult to justify on economics alone — the grid is already performing the storage function more cheaply. The argument for it is autonomy or an unreliable supply, and it should be made on those terms rather than on payback.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're hooked up to a reliable grid, there's no point having a battery system
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep630 labels the entire Ari Gerstman interview, including the host's long questions, with the guest's name; only the technical answers about curtailment, interconnection and microgrids are attributed to him.

ep583 similarly carries both sides under one label in places; the grid-control and operational-technology material is unambiguously Paul Zawada's, while the observation about the grid's scale is Dave Jones's and is attributed accordingly.
ep540 and ep495 label host questions with the guest's name; only unambiguous guest material was used.

This bundle contains a large volume of energy politics — carbon taxes, feed-in tariff levels, subsidy schemes and speculation about specific governments. All of it was excluded. What was kept is the physics, the control architecture, the failure modes and the measurement practice.
